slots.practicalActivity: Draft a one-page program charter for your own organization (or a realistic hypothetical mid-sized company): a one-sentence purpose tied to a real business pain point, a phase-one scope naming two or three specific data domains, an explicit 'out of scope for now' list, a named sponsor and approving body, and one measurable success criterion with a date. Then list the five to eight stakeholders this charter would actually affect and name which governance council or committee would have authority to approve it.
slots.deliverable: A one-page written program charter with a phased scope statement, plus a stakeholder list and the named approving council.

slots.practicalActivity: Design a stewardship program structure for the domains in your charter: name a steward for each domain, write their core responsibilities in one line each, and draft a one-page onboarding checklist a brand-new steward would actually follow in their first two weeks (what access they get, what training they take, what their first deliverable is).
slots.deliverable: A written stewardship assignment for each charter domain, plus a one-page new-steward onboarding checklist.

slots.practicalActivity: Write one real governance policy for a domain from your charter (a short statement of what must happen, who it applies to, and why), then write the standard and the step-by-step procedure that implements it -- the policy says what must be true, the standard sets the measurable bar, and the procedure says exactly how someone follows it day to day.
slots.deliverable: One written policy statement, one measurable standard, and one step-by-step procedure, all for the same governance rule.

slots.practicalActivity: Diagram the workflow someone follows to propose, review, and approve a new policy under your charter (who submits it, who reviews it, who signs off). Then write an escalation path for a policy violation found in the field (who gets notified first, what the time-to-response target is, and who makes the final call if the submitter and the reviewer disagree) and a one-line decision-rights statement naming exactly who is Accountable for that decision versus who is only Consulted.
slots.deliverable: A written policy-approval workflow, an issue-escalation path with a response-time target, and a one-line decision-rights statement.

slots.practicalActivity: Policies-and-process lab: assemble the policy, standard, procedure, approval workflow, escalation path, and decision-rights statement from the last two slots into one governance process pack for a single domain, then walk one hypothetical real-world violation of that policy through the entire pack end to end, from detection to final decision.
slots.deliverable: One consolidated governance process pack for a domain, plus a written walkthrough of one violation handled start to finish through it.

slots.practicalActivity: Write five governance KPIs for your program covering at least one data-quality metric (check pass rate, issue resolution time) and one adoption metric (percentage of critical data elements with a named owner, percentage of stewards actively using the catalog), each with a current baseline you estimate honestly and a target value with a date.
slots.deliverable: Five written governance KPIs, each with a baseline estimate, a target value, and a target date.

slots.practicalActivity: Sketch a one-page governance dashboard layout showing your five KPIs from last hour (one row per metric: current value, target, status color, owner), then write a one-paragraph definition of what 'success' means for your program at the six-month mark, stated in terms of those same KPIs moving, not in vague language.
slots.deliverable: A sketched one-page KPI dashboard layout plus a written six-month success definition tied to those same metrics.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a one-page executive status report for your program using your dashboard and KPIs: lead with the single most important number (not a list of activities), state what's on track versus at risk in plain business language, and end with one specific ask (budget, headcount, or a decision) the executive audience could actually say yes or no to.
slots.deliverable: A one-page written executive status report ending in one specific, decidable ask.

slots.practicalActivity: Take the stakeholder list from your Chapter 1 charter work and plot each one on a power/interest grid (high/low power, high/low interest), then write a one-sentence engagement approach for each quadrant (manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed, monitor) naming at least one real stakeholder from your own list in each quadrant you can fill.
slots.deliverable: A completed power/interest stakeholder grid with a named engagement approach for each quadrant.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a simple communication plan grid for your program (audience, message, channel, frequency) covering at least three of the stakeholder groups from last hour's grid, then outline a one-hour data literacy training session you'd actually deliver to one of those audiences, naming its three core learning objectives.
slots.deliverable: A communication plan grid with three audiences, plus a one-hour training outline with three learning objectives.

slots.practicalActivity: Write down one realistic form of resistance your own program would likely face (a business unit that sees governance as pure overhead, a team that doesn't want its data classified or reviewed) and draft the actual conversation you would have with that stakeholder: the concern you'd acknowledge first, the one concrete benefit you'd offer them, and the compromise you'd be willing to make without giving up the core policy.
slots.deliverable: A written resistance scenario with a drafted response naming the acknowledged concern, the offered benefit, and the held line.

slots.practicalActivity: Build a four-phase roadmap for your program (naming what gets done in each phase, reusing your Chapter 1-4 work as phase one) stretching out a realistic 12-18 months, then write a one-page business case for funding phase two: the cost of continuing to do nothing, the cost of the next phase, and the expected return stated in terms even a skeptical CFO would accept.
slots.deliverable: A written four-phase governance roadmap plus a one-page funding business case for its next phase.

slots.practicalActivity: Score your own program honestly against a simple five-level maturity scale (initial, developing, defined, managed, optimized) across three dimensions -- policy, measurement, adoption -- naming the real evidence behind each score. Then compare your scoring approach to the course's case study: what did the case-study organization do differently to move up one maturity level, and would that same move work for your program?
slots.deliverable: A three-dimension maturity self-assessment with evidence for each score, plus a written comparison to the case study's maturity jump.

slots.practicalActivity: Capstone review: assemble a complete program management package for your charter's domains -- the charter, the policy/process pack, the five KPIs and dashboard sketch, the stakeholder grid and communication plan, the roadmap, and the maturity self-assessment -- into one coherent document a new program lead could pick up and run the program from.
slots.deliverable: One consolidated written program management package covering charter, policies, KPIs, stakeholder plan, roadmap, and maturity assessment.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course, a student can launch and run a real data governance program end to end -- a charter and stakeholder plan, written policies with escalation paths and clear decision rights, a KPI dashboard and executive reporting, a change-management and training plan, and a funded multi-phase roadmap with an honest maturity assessment -- the operational program-management layer that turns this career path's governance concepts into something that actually runs at an organization.
